content:
Hello!

I have been working on a personal project of mine (without mathlib) and noticed that there are a few apparent inconsistencies between the interfaces for Int.lcm and Nat.lcm. I first noticed that the theorem lcm 0 x = 0is named Nat.lcm_zero_left for natural numbers but for integers it is duplicated as both Int.zero_lcm and Int.lcm_zero_left. There is no corresponding Nat.zero_lcm theorem for Int.zero_lcm.

It is the exact same situation for lcm 1 x = x, gcd 1 x = 1, and gcd 0 x = x, and their commutative versions. In all eight cases the theorem for integers has two copies, one with the "left/right" naming convention and one with the "infix" or "ordered" convention, while the corresponding theorem for natural numbers has only the left/right convention.

Is there a specific reason that it is like this? Should the theorems Nat.one_gcd, Nat.zero_gcd, etc. be added to the natural numbers, or should the Int.one_gcd, Int.zero_gcd, etc. series be deprecated? My intuition likes the ordered convention more than the more than the left/right convention

This is my first post in the public zulip chat, and I am very new to contributing to open source projects so I'm also wondering if this is something that I could make an issue or PR on github about this, or if this is inconsequential enough to be mostly ignored.

Note that you can write docs#Int.zero_lcm and docs#Int.lcm_zero_left , to make it easier to navigate.

Strictly speaking, this isn't a duplication, as one uses an implicit argument and one uses an explicit argument. The implicit version is also tagged with simp to be used in that tactic.

So in that sense its @Int.zero_lcm which is the same as Int.lcm_zero_left , except the simp tag, and note also that one of them uses a projection dot notation, so it isn't strictly left anymore in the sense of applying lcm with 0 as the left argument (even if it is the same in some sense, at the Expr level both the implicitness and the projection change things ) .

The question as to why the docs#Nat.lcm_zero_left is the one tagged with simp, and seemingly has no implicit version, is a fair one.

Ah that makes sense!

Is there a difference between putting @[simp] on an implicit or explicit version of a theorem?
Check out Implicit-arguments-and-transparency , but in short, yea there are some technicalities involved.
I'm skeptical about having these variants, even if the implicitness differs. Looks like @Julia Markus Himmel added them in lean4#7802, as variants of the Nat lemmas (that don't exist?)
I was probably confused about whether lcm is an infix operator for the purposes of the naming convention which led to me adding the duplicates by accident.

Feel free to create an issue on the lean4 issue tracker to clean up this inconsistency; I agree that this is worth cleaning up eventually, but to be honest right now there is so much stuff that is just completely missing that there aren't many cycles available for these kinds of consistency improvements at the moment.

Julia Markus Himmel said:

I was probably confused about whether lcm is an infix operator for the purposes of the naming convention

FWIW Eric Wieser said "I think we name things based on whether they're morally infix" :sweat_smile:

The standard library is not mathlib, so rules that apply to one do not necessarily apply to the other.

In this case, the standard library does follow the "morally infix" rule, but gcd isn't really used as an infix operator in mathematical practice, so probably we want to get rid of Int.zero_lcm and friends.
Isn't gcd usually spelled as (a, b)? This looks pretty infix to me (technically mixfix)
I don't think we should use different conventions for gcd and lcm.
